# Implementation

How code should look like?

## Some small rules

- Use explicit types where the language and project policy require them. Do not hide uncertainty behind dynamic escape types. For example, do not use `var` keyword in C#.
- Fix broken construction or wiring instead of adding silent fallbacks, no-ops, or legacy behavior.
- Do not extract a method merely to label a few statements when keeping them inline makes lifecycle or ordering clearer.
- Make a value's unit or representation explicit in its identifier when omission could cause misuse. Follow the project's naming convention with names such as `duration_seconds`, `DurationSeconds`, or `limit_fraction`.

## Research Before Building a system

When to apply: adding or replacing a system whose implementation approach is not established by the project, where existing software could supply required capabilities or resolve an unknown integration mechanism.

MUST inspect project code and current dependencies first. If they do not supply the required implementation or reference, search for existing implementations before choosing how to build the system.

Inspect source code or official documentation. Compare reuse, adaptation and a new implementation against required behavior, architectural fit, integration work, verification work, dependency constraints and license. Reuse MAY mean a library, an application extended through an adapter, or a mechanism learned from source. An existing implementation does not by itself establish that adoption requires less work.

For example, a new chat frontend needs session navigation, streamed responses, tool displays and file review. Inspect existing clients and component libraries before implementing those capabilities. Extending an existing application MAY avoid building several of them.

For example, subscription authentication requires a refresh mechanism that the available API documentation does not establish. Inspect a client supporting the same authentication route before inventing the protocol.

By contrast, changing a label, correcting a calculation in an established code path, or adding a field to an existing form does not trigger this rule.

For a boundary case, a candidate application supplies the desired widget but requires replacing session storage, model transport and build tooling. Compare that integration work with a component library or a local implementation; finding an existing application does not require adopting it.

Why: research can avoid rebuilding existing capabilities and reveal protocol constraints before implementation. Limiting the trigger to system choices and unresolved integrations avoids requiring external research for routine local changes.

## Keep Core Behavior Independent of Presentation and Its Host

When to apply: introducing or changing the boundary between application or gameplay behavior and a UI, engine scene, or host process.

MUST identify the behavior's state owner, required lifetime and required execution contexts before choosing the boundary. Derive these from the request and project contracts. Include established needs such as automated verification, simulation, frontend replacement or survival across a host reload; do not invent future requirements.

Presentation and host adapters MUST depend on core-owned operations and contracts. Core behavior MUST NOT require presentation implementations, UI objects or rendered properties to determine its results. Keep mutable state within its owning scope so separate executions do not share state accidentally.

For a new or changed boundary, verification MUST exercise the production core behavior without the presentation or host dependency that the boundary is intended to exclude. Use existing dependency checks to detect prohibited imports. Separate folders or class names alone do not establish independence.

For example, a game AI evaluates possible attacks. Live combat and simulation use the same damage and movement rules, while each battle owns its mutable state. Running the simulation requires no sprites or animation nodes.

For example, a desktop application must support replacing its GUI. Its session operations accept core-owned inputs and produce results or events; a GUI adapter translates between those contracts and widgets.

By contrast, a hover animation belongs in the widget that displays it. This rule does not require moving appearance-only behavior into a domain service.

For a boundary case, a single-process application can satisfy GUI independence through modules and direct calls. Introduce a separate process only when a requirement such as independent lifetime or shared access justifies the communication and lifecycle work.

For a boundary case, engine-provided math and data types may remain in gameplay code when they do not require presentation or scene services. Possible future multiplayer or saving does not require implementing networking, save formats or a plugin system now.

Why: tying core behavior or state to the first presentation or host makes another execution context require changes to that behavior. Explicit dependencies and scoped state preserve reuse without requiring an architecture for hypothetical features.

## Keep spec owned by the object whose state it.

For example, `Knockback` must not check whether a displaced `Entity` position is valid when `Entity` owns team/grid boundaries; it should request displacement through an operation such as `entity.apply_knockback(delta)`, and `Entity` must enforce the invariant by clamping position. Treat the opposite design as misplaced responsibility or domain-invariant leakage: it violates encapsulation and the Tell, Don't Ask principle.

For example, a game rule said that "Boss always have Sanity effect(an effect that make Boss immune to Debuff)". Bad implementation: in every class that inherits from the Boss class (where Boss is an abstract class), the agent calls `AddEffect(new Sanity())`. Good: this rule should be implemented in Boss class

## DRY in implementation

Developer request: "Create a tutorial for Level 1; the tutorial will consist of multiple steps, and at each step, highlight the buttons the player needs to click using a flickering animation."

Bad approach: Implementing the flickering animation logic repeatedly within each tutorial step.

Good approach: Coding a dedicated function or class for the flickering animation, then having the tutorial steps act as consumers of that logic.

Why: This principle also applies to game UI design; ideally, most buttons should share the same style and logic. Violating the DRY principle not only results in bloated code but also breaches an implicit game design requirement: consistency. No one designs a game where every button uses a different style.

## Editor Tool UI Names

When to apply: making UI, such as game UI, a Godot editor plugin or a Unity editor window.

- Every element the developer can point at shows its name in a tooltip on hover. Drawn items count too, such as a key mark or a playhead.
- The name comes from the tool's UI reference document. That document is canonical. Add a missing element to it in the same change.
- Set the tooltip delay to 1 second if possible
- This rule still apply to game UI but with nuance: Godot editor already have native tooltip in PlayMode, the tooltip shows Node's name when developer click at any Node

Why: Sometime developer want to report bug of an UI element or button, but they cannot remember the names of the UIs, and furthermore, the UIs were largely written by agents.

## Guard Placement

A guard belongs where the invariant is established, not where it is consumed. Scattering defensive checks across consumers is a programming error, not caution: it hides who actually owns the rule, and it makes an invariant that already holds look uncertain to the next reader.

Before writing any defensive check, name who guarantees the condition:

1. **The producer already guarantees it** — do not re-check. The check is dead code. Instead, state the guarantee at the source (doc comment on the property, method, or event) so consumers can rely on it.
2. **Nothing guarantees it** — fix the producer so it does. Do not compensate in every consumer.
3. **The value crosses a trust boundary** (user input, network payload, file contents, another process) — validate once at the boundary, then treat it as trusted inside.

The clearest smell is an event handler that re-reads the state the event just announced:

```csharp
// WRONG - the notification already means this is true
private void OnGameOver()
{
    if (!BoardUtils.IsGameOver()) return;   // dead code
    Idle();
    enabled = false;
}
```

## Method Extraction

Do not extract a method that is called once merely to label one to five statements. Keep those statements at the call site when seeing them inline makes the lifecycle, dependency, or execution order clearer.

## Required Dependency Policy: No Fallbacks

Treat serialized scene references, required components, initialized gameplay behaviours, and mandated effects as runtime invariants. Access them directly.

- Do not add `null` checks or early returns that silently skip required runtime dependencies.
- Do not mask a missing dependency with a fallback object, default value, warning, legacy behavior, or no-op.
- Let software report its normal runtime error when an invariant is broken so the debugger identifies the offending object and stack trace.
- Fix the scene, serialized data, initialization order, or caller contract that violated the invariant. Do not make the consumer tolerate the defect.
- Do not write required-dependency handling like this:
```gdscript
if dependency != null:
    use_dependency()
else:
    use_legacy_behavior()
```
- Right solution:
```gdscript
use_dependency()
```
That's it. You don't need to check for that error

## Keep the Trace When Code Handles a Failure

When to apply: writing code that catches an error, converts it to a return value, an exit status or a message, or passes it across a boundary such as a process, a tool result, an RPC, or an API that returns only success or failure.

A handled failure MUST stay traceable to its origin: the original error's type and message, its cause chain, its stack, and the operation and input that failed. Put that record where the person who debugs it reads: in the rethrown error (wrap it with `cause`, never replace it), in the log the program writes, or in a file that the message names. A shell script that exits non-zero prints the failing command, its exit status, and the path of any log that holds the details.

When a dependency reduces a failure to a Boolean or a code, call the lower-level operation that raises the real error, or record the dependency's limit where its result is used. MUST NOT retry, guess a cause, or report a generic message instead.

An expected outcome that the caller handles as a normal result, such as a search with no match, is not a failure under this rule.

For example, a save function returns `false` when the disk is full, and the caller reports "Save failed". The reader cannot tell a full disk from a read-only file. Good: the caller uses the save operation that throws, and reports `ENOSPC: no space left on device, write 'notes.txt'` with its stack.

For example, a test script launches a program that exits 1, and the script exits 1 with no output, while the details sit in a report file the script never mentions. Good: the script prints "program exited 1; failures in <scratchpad>/run-7/report.json".

The same record serves the agent when the developer reports an error. The agent MUST find the trace itself, in the program's logs, error files and saved records, and MUST NOT ask the developer to supply it. When no record holds the trace, the missing record is a defect under this rule: the agent reports it and fixes the code so the next failure keeps its trace.

For example, the developer reports that an app shows only "RuntimeError". Bad: the agent asks for the full error text. Good: the agent reads the app's log and finds the stack; when the app kept only the type name, the agent says so and makes the app save the message and stack in a file that the notice names.

Why: a failure without its cause makes the reader reproduce it to learn what the error already knew. On 2026-10-20, an editor save API reduced errors to `false`, and a workflow script exited 1 silently with its failures in an unmentioned report; each cost a separate investigation. On 2026-10-27, a chat app showed only `RuntimeError` for a failed turn, so the agent had to infer the cause by counting tool calls in the session record.

## Comment rules

- Comment non-obvious reasons, invariants, units, ordering, external constraints, and deliberate trade-offs. Do not restate the code.

## Automate Repeated Work

This is DRY applied to execution. [DRY](../AGENTS.md#drydont-repeat-yourself) covers the other half: one canonical owner for a fact.

When the same operation runs 3 or more times, build the mechanism that performs it, then run the mechanism. Doing the operation by hand repeats the lookups and the judgement calls with it, and each repetition can go wrong on its own.

For example, the developer asks the agent to migrate every `.prefab` file in a Unity project to `.tscn` in a Godot project. The agent converts all 12 prefabs by hand instead of writing a Python script that converts them. This violates DRY: the agent now looks up Unity YAML syntax once per prefab, and a rule it applies correctly to prefab 3 can be forgotten at prefab 9. The script states the mapping once and applies it 12 times identically.

For example, a change must be checked against 40 scenes. Write one headless script that opens each scene and reports the failures. Opening 40 scenes by hand repeats the same judgement 40 times and produces no record of what was checked.

For example, the same three shell commands run before every commit. They belong in one hook or one script, named once, not retyped per commit.

MAY skip the mechanism when writing it costs more than the work that remains: the operation runs twice, or each case needs a different decision that no rule covers. Say which of the two applies before doing the work by hand.

You will see that many rules above this is a narrow branch of DRY:
- [Treat Workflow Failures as Improvement Triggers](RuleMaintenance.md#treat-workflow-failures-as-improvement-triggers), write a rules so that future mistake won't appear again
- [An Unrelated File Opened Is Also A Correction](RuleMaintenance.md#an-unrelated-file-opened-is-also-a-correction), better project-scoped AGENTS.md, lower error chance

Why: repeated work hides its own cost. Each manual pass looks small, so the total is never compared against the one-time cost of the mechanism, and the mechanism is also the only artifact that survives the task.

## 16 child rule

When to apply: creating, moving, or splitting a file or folder in a project folder that the developer or an agent browses, such as source, tools, assets, data, or documentation.

A folder holds at most 16 direct children. Only folders the developer or an agent creates count: generated output, git-ignored files, and third-party folders such as `node_modules` or a vendored library do not.

Every folder has a meaning: the one thing that all of its children share, such as the feature they implement, the system they belong to, or the owner that edits them. The folder name states that meaning. A reader who knows what they are looking for picks the folder from its name without opening any file inside it.

When a folder would pass 16, look for the groups that already exist among its children and give each group its own subfolder. MUST NOT split only to pass the limit. Numbered parts (`Part1`, `Part2`), alphabetical ranges (`A-M`), and catch-all names (`Misc`, `Common`, `Other`) name no shared meaning, so they are forbidden. When the children share no meaning beyond the parent's, the folder is the exception: report it to the developer with the reason instead of splitting it.

For example, a `UI/` folder holds 25 scripts: 9 for the battle screen, 8 for the shop, and 8 widgets that both screens use. Split it into `Battle/`, `Shop/`, and `Widgets/`. By contrast, `UI1/` and `UI2/` pass the count and tell the reader nothing about which one holds the shop.

Why: the developer and the agent have no reliable memory of where a file lives, so the folder tree is how both find a file without reading many files. A folder with more than 16 children sends the reader back to scanning names one by one, and a folder without a shared meaning sends the reader into every subfolder.

# File Size Limit

Summary: Rules for splitting source-code and documentation files by responsibility when the pre-commit hook rejects their size.

These rules belong to [Implementation](Implementation.md). The [staged-file checker](../scripts/check_staged_files.py), run by the pre-commit hook, owns the numeric limit and counting method.

A file-size rejection is a signal to split responsibilities, not a target to satisfy through compression. Like the [16 child rule](Implementation.md#16-child-rule), this check supports maintenance through meaningful groups. The file-size check does not limit the expanded prompt or token count.

When the pre-commit hook rejects a file for its size:

1. Do not reduce readability by removing comments, collapsing formatting, shortening meaningful names, combining unrelated logic, or writing denser code.
2. Do not omit necessary information merely to pass the check.
3. Identify distinct responsibilities, concepts, sections, or components within the file.
4. Extract those responsibilities into separate, clearly named files.
5. Keep each resulting file cohesive and understandable on its own.
6. Update imports, references, navigation, indexes, or documentation links as needed.

A file may exceed the enforced size limit only when splitting it would create artificial fragmentation, excessive indirection, or reduce maintainability. In that case, explain why the exception is justified before proceeding and record the exception under [Shared Check Configuration](SharedChecks.md#configure-shared-check-exclusions-and-exceptions).

For example, split a rejected file when the file combines saving and UI responsibilities. By contrast, do not split a cohesive file merely because of its line count when the hook accepts its size.

Why: the hook can measure file size, but choosing meaningful responsibility boundaries requires judgment. Keeping numeric enforcement in the checker avoids duplicating details that the hook already enforces.

# Shared Check Configuration

Summary: Rules and configuration formats for shared file-size exceptions, generated-content exclusions, and folder-child exclusions.

These rules belong to [Implementation](Implementation.md).

## Configure Shared Check Exclusions and Exceptions

When to apply: adding third-party or generated content, adding engine sidecar files, or approving an exception to the [file-size limit](FileSize.md).

- MUST configure third-party and generated directories in the project-root `.agent-checks.json` under `exclude` when they would otherwise be checked.
- MUST configure committed third-party directories in the project-root `.folder-child-limit.json` under `third_party`. Configure engine-generated sidecar suffixes under `sidecar_suffixes` when they must not count as folder children.
- An approved exception to the [file-size limit](FileSize.md) MUST be recorded in `.agent-checks.json` under `line_exceptions`, with the repository-relative file path and a nonempty reason.
- MUST stage the configuration change with the content it governs, because the pre-commit hook reads configuration from the index.
- MUST NOT exclude authored project content merely to make a failed check pass. Fix the violation, or obtain approval for an exception permitted by the owning rule.

### Configuration Format

Both configuration files contain a JSON object. Add the needed keys to an existing file; do not replace unrelated settings.

Use repository-relative paths with `/` separators, such as `vendor/library`, not absolute paths or glob patterns.

In `.agent-checks.json`:
- `exclude` is an array of directory-path strings. Each entry excludes that directory and everything beneath it from source-character and Markdown-link checks.
- `line_exceptions` is an object mapping an exact file path to a nonempty reason string. The existing key name is retained for project configuration compatibility, but an entry now permits that file to exceed the character limit; it does not disable Markdown-link checks.

For example, after approval of the file-size exception:

```json
{
  "exclude": ["vendor/library", "generated"],
  "line_exceptions": {
    "scripts/Parser.py": "Approved: splitting the grammar table would separate entries reviewed together."
  }
}
```

In `.folder-child-limit.json`:
- `third_party` is an array of directory-path strings. Each listed directory counts as one child of its parent, but its contents are not counted.
- `sidecar_suffixes` is an array of literal filename-ending strings, including the leading dot. For example, `.meta` excludes files whose names end in `.meta`.

```json
{
  "third_party": ["vendor/library"],
  "sidecar_suffixes": [".meta"]
}
```

Omitted keys use the checker's defaults. These examples show the value shapes; they do not authorize exclusions or exceptions.

The checkers own the accepted formats and matching behavior: [check_staged_files.py](../scripts/check_staged_files.py) and [folder_child_limit.py](../scripts/folder_child_limit.py).

For example, a committed vendor library is excluded from source checks and identified as third-party content for folder counting. By contrast, a project-owned source file exceeding the character limit must be split by responsibility or receive an approved file-size exception; it is not third-party content.

Why: automatic checks still need project-specific scope. Recording that scope in configuration prevents agents from repeatedly encountering the same out-of-scope failures or bypassing checks to commit.

# Testing

Use the shared foundation in [AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md).

## Start With Workflow Verification

When to apply: selecting or extending automated verification for changed behavior.

Start verification through the production entry point for the changed workflow. Prefer one integration scenario that checks several related behaviors over separate tests for each function.

Reuse existing scenarios and fixtures before creating new ones. Minimize setup effort and additional test code without removing required behavioral checks. Executing a function does not establish that its behavior was checked.

Do not add unit tests merely because a function changed. Add another test method only when the workflow test cannot:

- Reach a required state.
- Check a required result.
- Reproduce a reported defect.

State the uncovered behavior before adding that method. A failing assertion requires investigation. It does not, by itself, justify changing the test method.

For example, an existing checkout scenario submits two items through the real checkout entry point and asserts the calculated total, payment status, and created order. When the price calculation changes, update the assertions in this scenario rather than creating a separate test for the calculation function.

By contrast, if the existing checkout scenario reports an incorrect total, investigate the failure through that scenario. The failed assertion does not justify creating another test method.

Do not replace a workflow test merely because it reports an incorrect total. Investigate that failure through the existing scenario.

Why: tests organized around functions can duplicate setup and checks. Workflow scenarios can check component interactions with fewer test files.

## Select Valuable Tests

Avoid tests for trivial getters, setters, constructors, passthroughs, and implementation details.

Test behaviour, not implementation.

## Do Not Reimplement Production Behavior

When to apply: constructing test fixtures, fakes, or expected results.

Apply DRY from the [shared foundation](../AGENTS.md) to test construction. Tests MUST execute the production implementation of the behavior they claim to verify.

Do not copy production algorithms, state transitions, or invariant enforcement into test helpers or fakes. A copied implementation can repeat the same defect without exercising the production code.

Fixtures MAY supply inputs and independently specified expected results. These are test data, not replacement implementations.

Fakes MAY supply scripted responses for dependencies outside the test's verification scope. They MUST NOT replace the behavior the test claims to verify. State which boundaries are fake when reporting integration coverage.

For example, a fake model can request Read while the real harness executes Read and returns its result. This verifies harness tool handling, not the model service.

By contrast, a test that claims to verify file editing cannot replace the production editor with a fake that writes the expected file itself.

Why: a passing test must establish production behavior, not merely agreement between test-owned substitutes.

## Test Only What the Branch Changes

When to apply: writing a test, and dropping or reverting a change that has tests.

A test stays only when it covers behaviour this branch changes. When a change is dropped or reverted, its tests go with it. A rule owned by another component, such as a shared system another developer maintains, is asserted by that component's tests, not again by a test of the code that relies on it. A test may still trigger that rule as a setup step, as long as it asserts only the branch's own behaviour.

For example, a branch changes how one game piece removes its own buff at a phase change. Its tests assert that removal. They do not assert that the effect system rejects a duplicate trait or promotes the next instance, because the effect system owns those rules and its tests cover them.

For example, a change to a passive is reverted after a policy merge makes it unnecessary, and the agent keeps the passive's regression tests as a separate commit. The commit adds tests for code the branch no longer changes, so it is dropped with the change.

Why: a leftover test from a dropped change pins behaviour nobody on the branch changed, and a test that re-asserts another component's rule fails when that owner changes the rule on purpose. Both cost review time and history without guarding anything the branch did.

## Representative Non-Test

Do not add a permanent test that sets a developer-only overlay's debug flag to `false` and only asserts that the overlay is hidden. This covers one trivial Boolean branch, is cheap to verify manually. Add automation only when the gate has meaningful lifecycle or state combinations, is shared by multiple tools, has regressed before, or can exercise the actual release artifact.

## Do Not Copy Tuned Numbers Into Tests

When to apply: a test asserts or uses a number that someone tunes for balance, feel, or performance, such as a unit's health, a price, a cooldown, an effect's strength or duration, a spawn interval, a timeout, or a retry count.

A tuned number has one owner: a named constant in production code, or an authored data file such as a Godot `.tres`, a Unity ScriptableObject, or a JSON config. It changes on every tuning pass. By contrast, the behaviour built on it stays the same: the unit attacks, the effect ends, the spawns keep their order. So a test pins the behaviour.

- Assert behaviour: who survives, whether a target is hit, that an effect expires, that a retry loop stops.
- When an assertion needs a tuned number, read it from its owner: write `assert_eq(armor, ARMOR_BONUS)`, not `assert_eq(armor, 40.0)`. Derive a value that depends on tuned numbers in the test, from the same owners: write `start_x + config.move_speed * seconds`, not a `3.0` worked out by hand.
- When the owner is a literal inside production code, such as `damage *= 2.0`, extract a named constant first, because a test cannot reference a literal.
- MUST NOT assert that an authored data file holds a particular value, such as `assert_eq(archer.max_health, 120.0)`. The file already is that value, so the test only repeats it.
- MUST NOT rely on a tuned value being zero or absent without reading it. For example, a test adds 40 armor and asserts `armor == 40`, which holds only while the unit's authored armor is 0. Read the starting value first, or use a fixture the test builds.
- A test MAY write its own numbers for inputs it owns: a fixture config it builds, the damage it deals, the grid size it creates. Keep test-only tolerances and timing margins explicitly named.

Why: a test that copies a tuned number fails on a balance change while no behaviour broke. The reader learns to update the number without reading the failure, and then the test stops catching real regressions. In a game project, raising one unit's health from 120 to 200 failed a test that only repeated the data file.

## Workflow Selection and Test Cost

[TestingWorkflow](TestingWorkflow.md) owns test execution, selection and regression-value criteria.

@TestingWorkflow.md

## Agent Tests Logic, Developer Judges Visuals

The agent MUST test every behavior that produces text it can read: return values, logs, files, process state, and messages between processes. When the product has a GUI, drive the layer under the GUI instead of asking the developer to click: call the handler, send the request, or run the code the button runs.

The agent MAY hand the developer only checks that need sight or taste: layout, readability, and whether a game looks or feels good. Whether an element is on screen is not one of them: [Query the GUI Before Asking the Developer to Look](#query-the-gui-before-asking-the-developer-to-look) owns that case.

Before asking for a manual test, state what the agent already verified as text. Ask the developer only for the visual part that is left, delivered as a capture under [Capture Visual Evidence for the Developer](#capture-visual-evidence-for-the-developer) when the project has a route.

For example, in a VSCodium chat extension that runs Claude through the Agent SDK, the check is "Claude answers, and the Read tool runs":

- Agent: a Node script calls the SDK's `query` with the same options as the extension and a stand-in `Read` tool. The script prints the tool name Claude called, the input the handler received, and the answer text.
- Developer: opens the chat panel and confirms that the answer and the "Ran Read" entry are shown.

For example, "Stop ends the `claude` process": the agent starts a query from a script, aborts it, and runs `pgrep` itself. Asking the developer to press Stop and run `pgrep` wastes a round trip on a check with no visual part.

**Why**: the agent works through text and cannot see the screen. The developer sees the GUI directly and judges it better than an agent does.

## Query the GUI Before Asking the Developer to Look

When to apply: a check concerns what a running GUI shows, and you are about to ask the developer to look at the screen.

A GUI framework exposes its widget tree to a debugger, and a widget tree is text. Find that channel and query it first. A screenshot says which of several states you are in; a query names the element, its class list, its computed style and its contents, which is what the fix needs.

Spend at most 10 minutes finding the channel. When none exists, name the channels you tried, then hand the check over.

| Runtime | Channel |
|---|---|
| Electron, VS Code, VSCodium | Launch with `--remote-debugging-port=<port>`, then the Chrome DevTools Protocol at `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/json/list`. `Runtime.evaluate` reads the DOM, `Input.dispatchKeyEvent` and `Input.dispatchMouseEvent` drive it. |
| A web page | The same protocol, or the session's browser tools. |
| Godot | The remote scene tree in the editor debugger, and `print` from `_process` into the log the agent reads. |
| Unity | The editor API through the `unityMCP` skill. |

Presence in the tree is not proof that the developer sees it. Read the computed style and the box: a node can carry text while its computed `display` is `none` and its box is 0 by 0. Report what is drawn, not what exists.

When two states differ only in what is drawn, change one input and query again. The pair is the evidence; a single reading of a broken state names no cause.

Hand over only what needs sight or taste: whether a layout reads well, whether a game feels good, whether a colour is right.

Why: the agent cannot see a screen, so it treated every visual question as the developer's. Most of them are not visual; they are queries against a tree the agent can read directly, and each hand-over costs a round trip and arrives as a picture the agent cannot act on.

## Capture Visual Evidence for the Developer

When to apply: a change has a visual part that the developer would otherwise check by launching the product and reaching the state by hand, such as a new character, an animation, an effect, a layout, or a UI flow.

Test the logic as text first, under [Agent Tests Logic, Developer Judges Visuals](#agent-tests-logic-developer-judges-visuals). Then capture the visual part and link it in the reply as a Markdown link to its absolute path in the session scratchpad, such as `[clip.mp4](<scratchpad>/video/clip.mp4)` where `<scratchpad>` is the absolute path that `$AGENT_SCRATCHPAD` holds, so the developer opens it with one click without launching the product. MUST NOT send it with the harness's file-sending tool: a link sits next to the caption that says where to look, and it opens in the developer's own player. The capture replaces the developer's manual session, not the logic test. Whether an element is drawn at all is a query under [Query the GUI Before Asking the Developer to Look](#query-the-gui-before-asking-the-developer-to-look), not a capture.

- **Image or video.** An image shows a state: a layout, a colour, a label. A video shows change over time: an animation, a transition, a sequence of steps. Send an image when nothing in the check moves.
- **Drive it through the production path.** A driver (a script, a scene, a test entry point) reaches each state through the code path the product uses. It also stages states that are slow or impossible to reach by hand, such as a skill with a long cooldown or a failed network call.
- **Off the developer's screen.** Render into a virtual display or an off-screen renderer. A headless mode that draws no frames captures nothing, so prove the renderer draws before relying on it. When no off-screen route exists, [Ask Before Taking the Developer's Machine](Execution.md#ask-before-taking-the-developers-machine) applies.
- **Own state only.** The driver runs on its own profile, save file, and settings, because the product may write on exit and overwrite the developer's data. The driver and its outputs go in the session scratchpad, under [Typical Project Structure](../AGENTS.md#typical-project-structure). An engine can load a driver from outside the project: for example, `godot-4 --path . /abs/path/Driver.tscn` runs a scene outside `res://`, and the scene's scripts still use the project's classes.
- **Mark each behavior.** The driver prints one line per behavior it shows, with its time in the video. Build the caption from those lines, so the developer knows where to look.
- **Short.** One video is at most 30 seconds. Split a longer showcase into one video per behavior group.
- **Check before linking.** The file has the expected size and duration, it is a format any player opens (PNG, H.264 MP4), and a frame taken at one marked time is not blank. A broken capture costs the round trip it was meant to save.

Find the project-owned capture route through the [Project Index](ProjectRules.md#project-index). A project with a GUI and no route gets one proposed.

For example, a new game character: the driver spawns it beside an enemy, then shows its walk, an attack, its skill, a hit, and its death in one 15-second video.

For example, a new button in an editor's side panel: the driver opens the panel, and one screenshot of it answers whether the button looks right. A video adds nothing, because nothing moves.

Why: checking a visual by hand costs the developer a launch, a route through menus, and a staged state, and some states cannot be staged by hand at all. A capture costs seconds of looking, and the driver reaches every state the same way each time.

# Testing Workflow

Summary: Rules for automated test execution, change-based selection, the 20-second mean budget for development verification, and whether regression coverage justifies its run time.

These rules belong to [Testing](Testing.md).

## Execute Tests by Default

Agents own automated test execution by default. Use [Automate Project-Lifetime Tests](#automate-project-lifetime-tests) for tests maintained for the project. For session-only tests, run the relevant fixture first and expand only when risk or focused failures justify it.

Leave physical-device checks, performance measurement, usability review, and release approval to the developer unless explicitly delegated.

A result is evidence only when the intended fixture was discovered and a nonzero test count executed. A skipped or silently excluded test script is a failure of evidence, even if the runner exits successfully.

A script that tests or reproduces a behavior prints every error it catches and exits non-zero when anything fails. Its cleanup MUST NOT call `exit(0)` or swallow the exception: a `finally { process.exit(0) }` turns a crash into a silent pass. Exit code 0 with missing output is a failure of evidence, not a pass.

## Automate Project-Lifetime Tests

When to apply: adding or maintaining automated tests intended to remain useful beyond the current session.

Maintained tests MUST have a documented automated entry point. Adding a maintained test MUST NOT automatically add its execution to every commit.

A project-owned selection command MUST select checks from the changed files using project-owned test-selection configuration. Selection MUST include directly changed tests. Explicitly classified non-executable changes MAY select only the applicable non-executable checks. An unmapped change MUST select the full relevant suite.

The pre-commit hook MUST NOT run tests; it runs only the staged-file checks. The agent runs the selection command once, after the last commit of the request, against the last commit, and runs exactly the checks it selects. The agent MUST NOT add, skip, or replace a selected check by its own judgement. It MAY run another check only to diagnose a failure.

For example, a request implements two features in two commits. The selection command runs once after the second commit, and its selection covers the files both commits changed.

Why: a hook runs the selected tests at every commit, so a request with two commits pays for two runs, and in one project a single run took 144 s. A command still selects from the changed files, so selection does not depend on the agent's judgement.

Changes to the test-selection configuration, shared test runner, or dependency configuration MUST select the full relevant suite unless the project defines and verifies a narrower dependency boundary.

The selector MUST print the selected checks and the reason for each selection, deduplicate checks, and execute them against the same candidate snapshot used for selection.

Workflows not selected for every commit MUST remain available through the project's test entry point. The project MUST state when those workflows are required, such as before merging or releasing.

Verification MUST test the committed files. When uncommitted changes could affect the result, run verification in an isolated checkout of the last commit. MUST NOT treat a passing test against different working-folder content as evidence that the commit passes.

A failed selected check MUST be fixed in a new commit, followed by another run of the selection command, before the final reply. When a blocker prevents the fix, the reply names the failing check. Each selected check MUST run for the same snapshot. MUST NOT repeat a passing check when its checked content, dependencies, configuration, and selection remain unchanged. Failed checks MAY be rerun to diagnose the failure; a later pass MUST NOT silently erase an earlier failure.

Tests that are only valid for the current session MUST remain in the session's scratch folder, under [Typical Project Structure](../AGENTS.md#typical-project-structure). MUST NOT add them to the project's permanent test workflow.

For example, a documentation-only commit runs the applicable staged-file checks without launching an editor when no executable behavior or test configuration changes.

By contrast, a passing run that included an unstaged storage fix does not verify a commit that omits the fix.

Why: verification must cover the committed behavior without repeating unrelated workflows or allowing uncommitted changes to hide a broken commit.

## Keep a Test Only When Its Regression Value Exceeds Its Run Time

When to apply: adding a test to the project's permanent tests, selecting a verification workflow, or reviewing verification time.

Treat development feedback time as a quality criterion alongside regression detection. Target an average end-to-end wall time of at most 20 seconds for each development verification run (lightweight verification). Measure from starting the verification entry point through selection, setup, process startup, execution and cleanup; parallel tests contribute elapsed wall time, not the sum of their durations. Report the sample count and environment with a measured mean; one run establishes only that run's duration. A project MAY set different budgets through an explicit project override with its reason.

First remove avoidable work, reuse supporting processes where test isolation permits, and select checks by affected workflow under [Automate Project-Lifetime Tests](#automate-project-lifetime-tests). When retaining every check would exceed the budget, development speed MAY take priority over additional regression coverage: remove checks whose regression value does not justify their cost, or move them to a documented event such as merge, release or dependency upgrade. Record the omitted coverage and the failure that could then go undetected; MUST NOT silently skip a selected check or describe unverified behavior as passing. Report an unresolved overrun with measured times rather than weakening assertions or test isolation merely to meet the clock.

For example, reuse one loaded test process across 40 cases while giving each case fresh storage; there is no reason to reload the same libraries 40 times unless a case verifies startup. By contrast, a test of crash recovery must exercise the crash and restart, so keeping its process alive would remove the behavior under test.

A permanent test costs its run time on every commit that selects it, for the life of the project. It pays back only when a later change breaks the behavior it checks. Verify a new behavior in the scratch folder first. Promote the test to the permanent tests only when at least one of these holds:

- Code that other tasks change often runs the behavior, so an unrelated change can break it.
- The behavior has regressed before.
- A break would stay unnoticed in daily use, or would damage data, such as a lost chat or a file written by the wrong owner.

Assume a later agent edits only the code its task names. A test of behavior that only that code runs, and whose break the developer sees on first use, stays in the scratch folder.

A permanent test whose behavior breaks only at a known event, such as an editor upgrade, runs at that event and not on every commit, under [Automate Project-Lifetime Tests](#automate-project-lifetime-tests).

For example, a new label shows the session id in the chat header. The agent checks it once through the editor, from a script in the scratch folder. Only the label's own code shows it, and a missing label is visible at once, so the script stays there.

For example, a change to how turn logs are written gets a permanent test, because every chat writes through that code, and a bad write loses history without any visible error.

For example, a test to check if prompt caching work properly, it should be pernament test, because the bad situation fail silently

Why: every permanent test was kept because it verified something once, so the suite only grew. In one project a typical commit ran 9 editor workflows and took 50–90 s, and the project is the developer's working tool, so a slow fix delays their main work.

# Authoring

Use the shared foundation in [AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md).

## Markdown Document Kind

When to apply: creating a documentation file, or adding a section to one.

A file has one main kind: the question its reader holds when opening it. The kind decides how the file is written, not which folder it goes in. The folder comes from the topic the file serves, under [16 child rule](Implementation.md#16-child-rule).

| Kind | Reader's question | Holds |
|---|---|---|
| How-to | How do I do this task? | Ordered steps for one kind of work, and the stop conditions met during them |
| Rules | What must hold, or what is the exact value? | Rules and contracts, each with its reason next to it, and lookup tables |
| Explanation | Why is it shaped this way? | Architecture, product vision, and the premise behind a design |

- The main kind is the kind that most of the file's sections answer. A section of another kind stays when the reader needs it at that point: the reason next to a rule, the command that runs a rule's check, a stop condition inside a step.
- A decision record's main kind is Rules: its Decision section states what must hold, and its Why section is the reason next to it.
- When a group of sections of another kind is read by a request that does not need the rest of the file, split that group into its own file and link to it.
- A project MAY add kinds for material these three do not cover, such as lessons. Project-specific conventions follow [ProjectRules](ProjectRules.md#project-index).

For example, a document holds three rules for how the save file is written, each with its reason, and the command that checks them. Its main kind is rules, and the reasons and the command stay in it.

For example, a migration guide holds nine fidelity rules and seven slice steps. A code review reads the rules without the steps, so the rules move into their own rules file and the guide links to it.

Why: a rule and its reason are read together. A layout that files the rule and its reason under two different kinds makes the reader open two files to apply one rule, and after [Documentation Audit](#documentation-audit) most documents that remain are rules with their reasons.

## Documentation Audit

Condition for the document to exist: Very simple, the documentation must contain information that is difficult to find in the code or is not present in the code at all. The description field will clearly show that.

Typically, the following common scenarios arise:

| Sentence | Where it goes |
|---|---|
| **Reason** that no code shows. A product goal counts: the audience and the intended experience are the reason behind every design that serves them | An ADR, the project's product-vision document for a product goal, or a code comment when only one file is affected |
| **Principle** that every instance of a kind must follow and that no code or lint checks. For example, the art style every character image follows | Its document, or the project `AGENTS.md` when almost every request needs it |
| **Flow** that no call chain from one entry point shows: it crosses a process or repository boundary, runs through a callback or event that another component fires later, or its source is out of reach (an LLM, an operating system kernel) | Pseudocode under [Explaining a Technique](Explanation.md#explaining-a-technique), in the document that owns the design. Name the real files and functions, so a reader can check the pseudocode against the code. |

**Delete** (no link replaces it; name the symbol directly instead):
- Anything code or data shows, including "feature X is not used". A flow counts as shown when a reader can follow it from one function by go-to-definition, however many files it spans.
- Dead design.
- A copy of another document.
- Rule IDs that no code or test uses.
- Task steps and status.

For example, a rules document lists every module with its folder and layer, copied from the manifest that the boundary lint reads. The manifest holds the list, so the table is deleted. The reason one layer exists stays, because no manifest shows it.

Why: a document that restates code drifts from it without any check failing, and every reader pays to open it. A document that holds only what code cannot say stays true, and stays short enough to read.

## Documentation Index

When to apply: adding, removing, moving, renaming, or re-describing a document in a project that has an index.

A documentation index is one committed file that lists every qualifying document with its relative path and a one-sentence description. It is the canonical entry point for document discovery, so that a reader never opens a document just to learn what it holds. [Route Through the Documentation Index](Execution.md#route-through-the-documentation-index) owns the reading half.

- The index is generated output. Never edit it by hand.
- Regenerate it in the same change that adds, removes, moves, renames, or re-describes an indexed document. A change that leaves the index stale is incomplete.
- Each entry's description answers the same question as the document's `Summary:` line. A description that does not let a reader decide whether to open the document is a defect in the description, not in the reader.

- Project-specific index configuration is reached through the [Project Index](ProjectRules.md#project-index).

For example, a project generates its documentation index from the `Summary:` lines of Markdown documents under `docs/`. Its Project Index links to the generation command and configuration.

# RuleMaintenance

Use the shared foundation in [AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md).

When to apply: reviewing, proposing, creating, or changing agent rules.

Most rules are added from agent mistake, and that mistake lead to consequences. Some rules come from developer preferences, or for the sake of consistency. For example, if we don't have a rule requiring Markdown filenames to be in PascalCase, the agent will name files arbitrarily; consistency makes reading the data faster.

Recommended structure of a rule:

```markdown
## Rule name

Write instructions here

For example, ...

For example, ...

Why:...
```

Most rules follow that structure; examples may be unnecessary if a rule is so straightforward that applying it requires almostly no reasoning.

When writing or editing rules, write for both agent and developer. The reason is developer must be able to judge whether the instruction solves the observed problem without weakening its meaning for the agent.

## Workflow

Why --> Examples --> Abstract instructions

Before writing the wording, check whether the reader can perform the required action using the rule and its explicit references. MUST NOT assume the reader has the author's session context or knows where an unnamed prerequisite is documented.

When an instruction requires a particular format, MUST provide the details needed to construct a valid input, or link to the canonical reference that provides them. An example MUST show the format when the format is what the reader needs to learn; explaining only the example's purpose is not enough.

For example, “put excluded directories under `exclude`” leaves the reader to guess the value type. Showing `"exclude": ["vendor/library", "addons/AnimationPanel"]` establishes that the value is an array of path strings. The instruction must still explain path matching or point to its canonical reference.

By contrast, “Open the file” does not need an explanation of files. A missing prerequisite is knowledge needed to carry out this instruction, not every fact related to its topic.

Why: the author can mentally fill in omitted details and mistake that understanding for a usable instruction. Checking the reader's required action exposes those omissions before the rule is written.

Place a rule by what triggers it, not only by its topic. When two owners seem to fit, identify when the agent must act and choose the owner responsible for that action.

For example, deciding who runs a check belongs to execution responsibilities; deciding what the check must verify belongs to testing.

Why: one topic can involve several responsibilities. The trigger identifies which responsibility owns the required action.

## Choose Global Rules or Skills

When to apply: choosing where to store a rule whose cross-project scope is already established under [Generalize from Why Line](#generalize-from-why-line).

- If more than half of requests need the rule, keep it in the global instructions.
- If half or fewer of requests need the rule, keep it in the global instructions when the complete rule, including examples and its reason, is 30 lines or shorter.
- If half or fewer of requests need the rule and the complete rule exceeds 30 lines, put it in a skill.
- Place a global rule in its existing responsibility owner. Do not shorten a rule merely to meet the 30-line cutoff.
- Base frequency on available request history or an explicit developer expectation. If neither establishes which side of half applies, ask the developer before choosing.

For example, a language rule needed in every reply stays global regardless of its length. A document-conversion workflow needed in one request out of ten belongs in a skill when its complete instructions exceed 30 lines. By contrast, a rule that applies only to one project is outside this choice.

Why: these cutoffs are developer-selected placement criteria. Global rules are loaded even when unused; a skill adds a description and an activation step. Keep instructions global when frequent use or a length of at most 30 lines makes that trade-off worthwhile.

## Use Project AGENTS.md as a Temporary Owner

When to apply: a project-scoped rule is needed, but its canonical owner within the project is not yet clear.

The project `AGENTS.md` MAY temporarily own the rule. Mark the placement as temporary and state which ownership decision remains unresolved.

Once the canonical owner is established, move the rule there. If automation fully enforces the rule, remove the duplicate instruction. Leave a link in the project `AGENTS.md` only when needed for routing.

For example, an asset-naming rule may temporarily live in the project `AGENTS.md` while the project decides which document owns asset requirements. Once that owner is chosen, move the rule there. By contrast, do not use temporary placement when an existing document already owns asset requirements.

Why: a needed rule must remain discoverable while ownership is unresolved, without turning temporary placement into a second canonical copy.

## Treat Workflow Failures as Improvement Triggers

When to apply: the developer undoes, rejects, or redoes a result that an agent produced, in this session or an earlier one, or points out a step the agent skipped. A question that comes from the developer not knowing an area gets an answer, and nothing is recorded.

For example (an undo with an unstated reason). The developer writes: "I no longer want markdown guides for testing this Entity. Create a scene that demonstrates its features, and the right arrow shows the next feature." Bad: the agent builds the scene and ends the turn. Good: the agent infers the reason from the profiles: the agent executes fast, so a driver scene stages each state in one frame (a Card dragged to a position, many Entities spawned, an Effect applied), while a guide makes the developer click through every setup step by hand. Testing is not specific to this Entity; every later feature is tested the same way. So the agent records reusable knowledge for future testing: manual checks in this project are stepped scenes, not guides, with the route recorded where [Capture Visual Evidence for the Developer](Testing.md#capture-visual-evidence-for-the-developer) says a project keeps it.

For example (an oversight). The developer writes: "You forgot to update the testing documentation to reflect the new changes." Bad: the agent updates the document and ends the turn. Good: the agent updates the document, then diagnoses why it was missed. Possible causes: nothing links the changed code to the document (routing), no tool lists what references the changed symbol (no LSP reference search), or no workflow step says that a change to this code also updates its testing document (a missing rule). The agent fixes the cause it found.

For example (a question that is not a correction). The developer asks: "Why does this passive remove every Camouflage?" The agent reads the code and the design. When the design requires it, the agent explains and records nothing. When the design gives no reason, the result was wrong, and the question is a correction.

For example (a project fact). The developer says a GUT suite the agent reported as passing never ran. The cause is that `-gtest=` takes a path relative to the project root, and the agent passed a path relative to the test folder, so the runner exited 0 with zero tests. Record in the project's `AGENTS.md` that a GUT result counts as evidence only when the printed test count is nonzero.

For example (a global step). The developer asks why a session list UI is empty. The agent reads the session files, the index and the viewer cache, finds all three healthy, report that agent cannot reproduce the issue and asks for a screenshot. The developer answers that the agent should have a way to inspect the GUI. Nothing about that repository was missing: the agent skipped a step that applies to any project with a GUI, so it became [Query the GUI Before Asking the Developer to Look](Testing.md#query-the-gui-before-asking-the-developer-to-look).

For example (nothing to record). The agent mistypes a path in one sentence then corrects it in the next and this only happen with probality under 5%

For example (nothing to record). Initially, the developer wanted to limit each harness turn to a maximum of 15 minutes, but later changed the requirement to a token budget limit. There is no lesson to be learned here; both requests were simply directives, and the agent was not required to evaluate the underlying reasons for the requests.

For example, a bug appear, this is maybe a testing activity defect: test is too weak for detecting the bug. After fixing the bug, agent should take notice on current testing rules

Why: a fix repairs this session, a record repairs every session after it. Without this step the agent fixes each correction separately, and the same cause returns. In one observed session, three corrections that shared one cause were fixed one by one, and the cause was recorded only after the developer named this rule.

### An Unrelated File Opened Is Also A Correction

When to apply: you read a file, and it held nothing the task needed.

Two causes produce that read: the agent chose badly, or the project routes badly. The second cause can be fixed more easily with a rule. A routing defect is one of:

- The project has no documentation index, so the only way to learn what a document holds was to open it.
- The index entry's description does not describe the document, or it is stale.
- The document mixes kinds, so one sentence cannot describe it. See [Markdown Document Kind](Authoring.md#markdown-document-kind).
- project-scoped `AGENTS.md` or a document links to a file that was renamed, moved, split, or deleted.

For example, a task about the build pipeline ends with the agent opening six files under `tools/` because no document names which one runs first. Nothing is stale; the routing simply does not exist. The fix is an entry in `AGENTS.md` naming the entry point.

## The Why Line

Rule may carries a `Why`. It states the reason the rule exists. When the reason is a temporary condition, such as a bug, a missing tool, or a deferred task, the `Why` names that condition, so a reader can tell when the rule becomes obsolete. Rule is solution for "why", and that rule maybe not right solution

For example:
- Bad: `[Override] Tests are executed manually by the developer.`
- Good: `[Override] Tests are executed manually by the developer. Why: UnityMCP runs every test even when the agent selects only some of them. Fixing it is a deferred task.`

The bad form gives no reason, so the next developer or agent cannot tell whether the rule still matters, and may delete it while the bug still exists, or keep it forever after the fix. The good form says what to check: once the UnityMCP task is finished, the override can go.

## Generalize from Why Line

Start with the cause of the observed failure, or the reason stated in [The Why Line](#the-why-line). Choose the narrowest scope in which that cause or reason applies.

Evidence MUST support both the cause or reason and the proposed scope. Similar outcomes alone do not establish a shared cause. A `Why` line states the reason; it does not prove it.

Use the following table to choose the owner and check the evidence needed for that scope:

| Scope | Owner | Evidence needed |
|---|---|---|
| One place in the code | A code comment | The case itself |
| One project | The project `AGENTS.md` or document | The cause lies in this project's code, data, tools, or team |
| One tool used across projects | The skill for that tool | The cause lies in the tool, and the tool behaves the same in every project |
| Any project | A global rule | The cause lies in how the agent works, not in any code, and a second case in a different context can be named without changing the cause |

Before writing the rule, check it:
- The trigger is something the agent can observe in the conversation or the files, such as a kind of message or a file change. A judgement such as "the agent's fault" or "important" is not a trigger, because the agent decides it differently each time.
- The trigger identifies the conditions where the cause or reason applies, not merely a similar outcome.
- Include an example where the rule applies and one where it does not. For a rule that applies across contexts, include at least two applicable examples from different contexts, supported by evidence of the same cause or reason. A rule confined to one place does not require a second context. Invented examples MAY illustrate a rule, but MUST NOT count as evidence for widening its scope.
- Each word such as `every`, `any`, `always`, or `never` MUST be supported by evidence for the scope it claims.
- When an existing rule already covers the case, extend that rule instead, under [DRY](../AGENTS.md#drydont-repeat-yourself).

For example (a trigger that is too wide). After a session where corrections went unrecorded, an agent proposes: "a developer message that questions a result counts as a correction". A question also comes from a developer who does not know an area, so the rule would record a lesson from every explanation. The narrower trigger: "a question is a correction only when answering it shows the result was wrong."

For example (a scope that is too wide). In a game project, an agent changes six consumers of an effect on the assumption that the effect can hold several instances, and the project's effect system allows only one. A global rule "check the data model before every change" restates good practice and prevents nothing specific. The cause lies in one project's effect system, so the record is a project fact

For example (the right global scope). An agent asks the developer to look at a GUI for visual testing instead of querying its widget tree. The cause is the agent's habit, and the same habit appears in an editor extension, a web page, and a game, so it is a global rule, with some adoption in each project

Why: an agent generalizes from one case by default, and a rule that is too wide fires where it does not fit. A wrong rule then costs every session that loads it, while the mistake it came from cost one session.

## Examples in a Rule

When to apply: writing or revising an example in an agent instruction.

A reader understands the example from common knowledge plus the concept the rule teaches. Before writing it, test it: can the reader understand the rule recalling a fact from another field? If not, choose another example.

- An example MUST NOT depend on a project, repository, specific vendor or session. Global rules load at the start of every request, so the reader has no outside context.
- Prefer a setting from daily life or general computing over a setup sentence such as "we are in a game where ...". Use a setup sentence only when no common setting shows the mechanism, or when the rule is about that setting.
- An example MUST include the context needed to understand why the rule applies: the relevant situation or request, the condition that affects the choice, and the action or result that illustrates the rule.
- When an example comes from a project, repository, vendor, or session, explain the necessary facts within the example or choose a self-contained setting.
- Include only context that changes how the reader interprets or applies the rule. Common knowledge does not need an explanation.

For example, an example about a hidden premise uses "after a system update, the laptop battery drains faster". It needs only an update and a battery. By contrast, "a game froze while an asset import ran" needs three facts from game engines first: what an asset import is, that it competes with the game for CPU and disk, and whether the game's log would record that.

For example, an example about a size that needs a number uses "a larger file takes longer to download", not "a larger texture atlas takes longer to import". Both show size and time, but the second also makes the reader know what a texture atlas is.

You can take examples from any source (whether from the session itself or ones you come up with yourself), provided they meet the aforementioned conditions.

For example, a rule distinguishes a requested outcome from an implementation step. “Changing the converter is not a second outcome” leaves the reader to guess what was requested. Instead, write: “The developer wants exported documents to open in another application with text and images preserved. Propose that result; changing the converter is a possible way to achieve it, not a separate outcome.”

By contrast, “A download contains 100 MB and the connection transfers 10 MB per second, so the transfer takes about 10 seconds, excluding overhead” already supplies the facts needed to illustrate a time estimate. The example needs no project history or explanation of what a download is.

Whether an example supports a rule's scope is governed by [Generalize from Why Line](#generalize-from-why-line).

Why: an author remembers the omitted situation and can mistake a fragment for a complete example. Supplying the facts that affect the choice lets a reader understand and judge the example without the author's session context.

# Bandwidth Minimization

## Project Brief

Modern Issues in Computer Science, major assignment 2 (BTL 2). The project compares exact SAT, constraint programming (CP), and integer linear programming (ILP) approaches to the graph Bandwidth Minimization Problem. It produces the solver code, the experiment results, and the group report. Nguyen Thanh Binh is Member 3 (ILP).

## Project Index

| Question or task | Resource |
|---|---|
| Who owns what, mandatory scope, completion criteria | [Task.md](Task.md) |
| Mathematical problem and encoding notes | [docs/Problem.md](docs/Problem.md) |
